newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's opposition, students march for democracy.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's opposition, students march for democracy.

text.p: Opposition leaders led tens of thousands of supporters through the dark, chilly streets of Belgrade on Thursday, vowing to continue protests until democratic reforms are in place and their victory in Serbia's local elections are accepted.

"The number of people has not diminished in any way," opposition politician Zoran Djindjic told marchers converging on the city centre. "Our objective is the democratisation of Serbia, and anything less would be an insult to all these people."

Police kept a low profile again on the 75th day of demonstrations, making no attempt to halt or divert groups of pedestrians -- each several hundred strong and all wrapped in brighly-coloured anoraks, scarves and woolly hats against the biting cold -- heading to Republic Square.

Residents opened their windows en route and waved to those below, some banging pots and pans in a cacophany of solidarity, from whistles and cheers to impromptu singing and drumming. The mood was generally festive.

At the square itself, fireworks burst overhead. A cordon of anti-riot police in helmets and carrying shields and batons stood quietly at one end to deter the protestors, some of them holding children on their shoulders, from moving south into the government and business district.
Witnesses estimated the number of demonstrators at about 50,000.

Earlier in the afternoon some 15,000 students demanding political and educational reform filled the streets and disrupted traffic when they too marched on the railway station. Plainclothes police watched, but made no attempt to interfere.

Both students and the three-party opposition Zajedno (Together) alliance share the demand that the opposition victories in local elections on November 17 in 14 Serbian towns, including Belgrade, be recognised.

Investigators from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have concluded that the polls, annulled by President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists on grounds of "irregularities", were fairly won.

In what some political analysts saw as a conciliatory gesture testing the political atmosphere, Yugoslav federal President Zoran Lilic said the opposition victories should be recognised if that was the will of the people.

The election results should be recognised "wherever the will of the people has won and enable the opposition to constitute local government because it is in the interest of the stabilisation of Serbia and also of Yugoslavia," he said.
Lilic, whose duties are ceremonial, is often seen as a mouthpiece for Milosevic. He made a similar remark early on in the crisis, but it was swiftly forgotten.

An uncompromising note was struck on Thursday when the government adopted a recommendation by the Education Ministry to withhold state funds from universities and schools because of "disruptions", the official Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said.

Belgrade university, which has been the source of much of the dissent in the capital in recent weeks, has virtually stopped functioning while about 600 schools across Serbia have shut. Schoolteachers are on strike, mainly for better pay and conditions as well as educational reforms.
If enacted, political analysts say, suspending the cash could make life difficult for those among the protesting students who rely on state subsidies for accommodation and food as well as fees.
While Milosevic had stayed silent on opposition demands, discontent has spread. Belgrade lawyers said they would strike from Thursday until the opposition's election wins are accepted.
In Washington, the U.S. State Department said Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia all committed human rights abuses last year, especially of ethnic minorities.
In Serbia, the government's rights record "continued to be poor", the annual worlwide report said.
The Belgrade-based independent news agency Beta said on Thursday at least 26 ethnic Albanians were arrested by police in Serbia's Kosovo province over the past three days.

Kosovo has long been regarded as a potential flashpoint that could wreck Balkan peace efforts. In 1989 Serbia removed Kosovo's autonomy on the grounds that the region's majority Albanians were preparing to secede.
